clue.text: Provide with flexibility

definitions.meaning: to furnish or give what is needed
in a supple, pliant way: an adverb formed from supple

explanation.surface: An instruction to give something while staying adaptable.
explanation.walkthrough: The same spelling is two words: the verb meaning provide, and a rare adverb from 'supple', pronounced SUP-lee.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to furnish, while the adverb, built on 'supple', means in a pliant manner.

clue.text: The price of some asses in old Rome.

definitions.text: The price of some asses in old Rome.

parts.words: The price of some asses in old Rome.
parts.note: an 'as' was a Roman copper coin; the coin worth two and a half of them is meant, not the cost of donkeys

explanation.surface: What donkeys cost in ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asses' looks like donkeys but is the plural of 'as', a Roman coin; the answer was worth two and a half asses.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman silver coin valued at two and a half asses.

clue.text: Pelts with Jamaican fruit

definitions.meaning: allspice, called Jamaica pepper, is the berry of a Caribbean tree

explanation.surface: Someone throws Caribbean produce at people.
explanation.definitionFit: To pepper is to pelt with shot; Jamaica pepper is the allspice berry.

clue.text: Lose face by appearing distant?

explanation.surface: Being humiliated through seeming aloof.
explanation.definitionFit: Humiliation diminishes you in others' eyes; a far-off object seems tiny.

clue.text: Draws, showing art's involved with tact

indicators.note: letters that are involved with each other get tangled, so these words are mixed up together

parts.note: art's is read as the plain letters of arts

explanation.surface: Someone's artistic skill combined with diplomacy wins people over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved with' tangles ARTS and TACT together into the eight letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a crowd is to pull it in, a synonym of pulling people towards you.

clue.text: Tales suggesting that the man of property made some sound profit?

definitions.text: Tales suggesting that the man of property made some sound profit?

parts.words: Tales suggesting that the man of property made some sound profit?
parts.note: Galsworthy's novel sequence opening with The Man of Property; the family name heard as 'foresight', which makes a sound profit

explanation.surface: Stories implying a property owner earned a solid return.
explanation.walkthrough: The Man of Property is the first book of Galsworthy's sequence; the family name sounds like 'foresight', the shrewdness that would make a sound profit.
explanation.definitionFit: Galsworthy's chronicle of an upper-middle-class family, beginning with The Man of Property.

clue.text: Queer University type for a dance

parts.note: rum is old British slang for odd or queer
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a university graduate

explanation.surface: An odd sort of student goes dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance.

clue.text: Little room in one for an artist

parts.note: a cell is a small room
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A small room in a building is set aside for a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Benvenuto Cellini was the Italian Renaissance goldsmith and sculptor.
explanation.definitionFit: Benvenuto Cellini was a Florentine sculptor and goldsmith.

clue.text: Time's tool

parts.note: Father Time is pictured carrying a long curved blade for cutting

explanation.surface: An implement used by Time.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Time is traditionally shown carrying a long-bladed mowing implement.

clue.text: Auntie's rural brood

parts.note: an aunt's children are one's relatives of that kind, and rural ones are unsophisticated visitors from the provinces

explanation.surface: An aunt's children living in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase names unsophisticated people from the provinces, but read literally it is an aunt's offspring who live in the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Unworldly provincial relatives are literally an aunt's children from the countryside.

clue.text: University man has lost freshness

parts.note: a student no longer in the first, 'fresh' year at college: freshness lost means the freshman stage is over

explanation.surface: A student has grown stale.
explanation.walkthrough: In American usage the first-year student is a freshman and the second-year student has left that freshness behind.
explanation.definitionFit: An American second-year student is the one who is no longer a freshman.

clue.text: My round in the style of Eastman

indicators.note: one piece goes round another, so these letters wrap the next piece

parts.note: taken as written
a la, from French, means in the style of

explanation.surface: Someone buys drinks in the manner of a man called Eastman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastman' looks like a surname, as in George Eastman of Kodak, but it means a man from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Malay peninsula is a man from the East.

clue.text: Essayist makes men sore

indicators.note: the letters following make up something new when rearranged, so 'makes' is the signal to reorder

explanation.surface: A writer of essays irritates men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' tells you to rearrange MEN SORE; Ralph Waldo Emerson was the American essayist.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson was a famous American writer of essays.

clue.text: Shandy's prophetic servant

parts.note: the servant of the Shandy family in Sterne's novel Tristram Shandy, who shares a name with an Old Testament prophet

explanation.surface: A drinker's servant foretells the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shandy' is not the British beer-and-lemonade drink but Laurence Sterne's novel Tristram Shandy; the servant there shares a name with the shortest book of the Old Testament prophets.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shandy household's manservant bears the name of a minor Hebrew prophet.

clue.text: Plotter assailed with envy

parts.note: a conspirator against Julius Caesar, called 'the envious' by Mark Antony in Shakespeare's play

explanation.surface: A schemer is consumed by jealousy.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony, showing Caesar's cloak, says 'See what a rent the envious Casca made'.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the conspirators who stabbed Julius Caesar, labelled envious in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: Sinister monk gets Abyssinian Prince introduced

parts.note: Ras is an Ethiopian title for a prince or chief
put in means introduced

explanation.surface: A menacing monk acquires an Ethiopian nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: Abyssinia is the old name for Ethiopia, where a ras is a prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Grigori, the mystic who held sway over the last Tsar's court, is remembered as a sinister holy man.

clue.text: United Nations surplus to cause lack of equilibrium

parts.note: a balance is an amount left over

explanation.surface: UN overspending threatens to unsettle things.
explanation.definitionFit: To unbalance something is to throw it off its steady state.

clue.text: Emphasizes that some teachers want the motorway

indicators.note: to want is to lack, so these letters are missing

parts.note: mistresses are female schoolteachers
the M1 is Britain's first major motorway, written MI

explanation.surface: Some teachers press for a motorway to be built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'want' means lack: MISTRESSES without MI. The M1, London to Leeds, is Britain's main north-south motorway, with 1 written as I.
explanation.definitionFit: Stresses as a verb means lays weight on, a synonym of accentuates.

clue.text: The little devil's within the law, beyond question

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
licit means lawful

explanation.surface: A mischievous child is behaving legally, without a doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: Implicit faith is absolute, a synonym of unquestioning.

clue.text: Many a French Hamlet, for instance, proves worldly

parts.note: M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many
un is French for a
Hamlet was a prince of Denmark, so a Dane

explanation.surface: Lots of French villages turn out to be sophisticated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet' looks like a small village but is Shakespeare's Prince of Denmark.
explanation.definitionFit: Mundane means of this world, earthly rather than spiritual.

clue.text: Large high tension loop

parts.note: big means large
HT is the electrical abbreviation for high tension

explanation.surface: A big electric cable loop carrying high voltage.
explanation.definitionFit: A bight is a loop or slack curve in a rope, as sailors use the word.

clue.text: Enchantment of the love of France, noted above

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece above another comes first

parts.note: G is a musical note
l'amour is French for the love

explanation.surface: A romantic French spell is described in a written note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above' works because this is a down answer: G sits on top of LAMOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Glamour originally meant a magic spell, a synonym of bewitchment.

clue.text: Teeth ? A new gas for extraction

indicators.note: extraction is drawing something out, so letters are drawn from inside these words

explanation.surface: A dentist offers a new anaesthetic gas before pulling teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: The dentistry picture is the decoy: 'for extraction' draws the letters out of teETH A NEw.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethane is a colourless hydrocarbon, an example of a gas.

clue.text: Scramble, Anne, out of the back of the car

indicators.note: to scramble is to jumble, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Anne is told to hurry out of the rear seat of the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scramble' reads as 'hurry' but jumbles ANNE OUT. The answer is the rear passenger section of an early open motor car.
explanation.definitionFit: On early motor cars the tonneau was the rear passenger compartment.

clue.text: And here, classically, is the science of a moralist

parts.note: et is Latin for and
hic is Latin, the classical language, for here

explanation.surface: In Latin terms, this is where moral philosophy lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classically' means in Latin and covers both words: ET is 'and', HIC is 'here'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a system of moral principles, the study of right conduct.

clue.text: Rescue from wild gales round Virginia

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the next piece
wild means the letters run riot into a new order

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for the US state Virginia

explanation.surface: Saving people from fierce storms around the Virginia coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' jumbles GALES into SALGE, and 'round' places it around VA.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvage is rescuing property, especially a ship or cargo, from loss.

clue.text: Have a go, confound it

parts.note: a bash is a go or attempt, as in 'have a bash'

explanation.surface: An exasperated 'have a try, damn it'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confound it' reads as an oath; 'it' only links. 'Have a bash' is British for 'have a go'.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash someone is to disconcert or embarrass them.

clue.text: Cleverly contrived to go in, in use

definitions.text: Cleverly contrived to go in, in use

indicators.note: words cleverly contrived are rearranged, so the letters following are reordered

explanation.surface: Something designed smartly so it slots in while working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleverly contrived' rearranges GO IN IN USE; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ingenious is inventive and cleverly devised.

clue.text: Eric's in difficulty in the river-some task!

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, England

indicators.note: letters in difficulty are thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Eric's taken as its letters

explanation.surface: Eric is struggling in the water: quite an effort!
explanation.walkthrough: 'in difficulty' turns ERICS into ERCIS, and 'in' puts that inside EXE, a river in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An exercise is a set piece of work or practice task.

clue.text: Defies hair-fashions

definitions.meaning: styles of facial hair grown on the chin

explanation.surface: Someone flouts the rules through their haircuts.
explanation.definitionFit: To beard someone is to confront them boldly; as a noun it is a growth of chin whiskers.
